title: Study supports FDA approval of dolutegravir for HIV treatment in newborns
content:
An international study conducted through the International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials (IMPAACT) Network, involving researchers at the University of California San Diego, helped inform the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s recent approval of dolutegravir. This second-generation integrase inhibitor is now approved for treating human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) in newborns from birth.

The study, published in The Lancet HIV, identified a specific dosing regimen that achieves appropriate drug levels in full-term newborns. These findings support the use of dolutegravir to treat HIV from the first days of life.
summary: An international study through the IMPAACT Network helped inform the FDA's recent approval of dolutegravir for treating HIV-1 in newborns. The research, published in The Lancet HIV, identified a dosing regimen that achieves appropriate drug levels in full-term newborns.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Common multiple sclerosis treatment linked to bowel disease risk
content: A study led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet, published in JAMA Neurology, indicates that multiple sclerosis patients treated with rituximab face an increased risk of developing inflammatory bowel disease, specifically Crohn's disease. This first large population-based study in the field notes that while the risk is elevated, the absolute probability remains low.
summary: People with multiple sclerosis (MS) who are treated with rituximab have an increased risk of developing inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's disease, although the absolute risk remains low. This is according to the first large population-based study in the field, led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and published in JAMA Neurology.
author: Medical Xpress

title: 40.5% of U.S. High School Students Report Binge Eating in Past 30 Days
content: A study published online on October 15 in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report found that 40.5% of U.S. high school students experienced binge eating at least once in the previous 30 days.
summary: The prevalence of binge eating at least one day in the past 30 days is 40.5% in U. S.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Intermittent fasting and exercise improve fat loss and fitness in 12‑week obesity trial
content: A research team led by the Joint University Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at the University of Granada, in partnership with the Granada Institute for Biomedical Research and the Biomedical Research Network Center, examined the impact of combining intermittent fasting and supervised exercise on people with obesity. The study was conducted as part of the TEMPUS project, a 12‑week obesity trial.
summary: Intermittent fasting and exercise improve fat loss and fitness in 12‑week obesity trial.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Imaging study links several schizophrenia symptoms to a single brain signal
content: A new study suggests that a single brain signal may explain a range of seemingly unrelated schizophrenia symptoms. The research addresses the condition’s diverse manifestations, which include perceiving the world differently, acting on surroundings differently, and speaking in ways that are hard to follow.
summary: Schizophrenia is often described as a list of separate problems. People may perceive the world differently, act on their surroundings differently or speak in ways that are hard to follow.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Nurses are an important resource in Swedish bowel cancer screening
content: A study from Karolinska Institutet, published in Endoscopy, reports that colonoscopies performed by specially trained nurses within the Swedish bowel cancer screening program are of at least the same quality as those conducted by doctors. The findings suggest that nurses could help address the increasing demand for examinations in the national program.
summary: Nurses are an important resource in Swedish bowel cancer screening.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Rock plunging 90km into Earth reveals unexpected temperature pattern
content: Scientists in Papua New Guinea discovered a rock that plunged over 90 kilometers beneath Earth’s surface. The sample revealed a temperature pattern that shifts from unusually hot to relatively cold, challenging established theories of Earth’s interior. This finding could transform understanding of tectonic plate movements, earthquakes, and volcanoes.
summary: Scientists in Papua New Guinea discovered a rock that penetrated more than 90 kilometers beneath the surface, exposing a shift from hot to cold conditions. This finding challenges established theories of Earth's interior and could transform understanding of tectonic movements, earthquakes, and volcanoes.
author: Science Daily

title: AI analysis of Reddit posts finds unexpected symptoms from unapproved retatrutide
content: Researchers analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and identified unexpected symptom reports linked by users to unapproved versions of retatrutide. These reports included increased appetite, sleep disturbances, and elevated heart rates. The findings differ from clinical trial results, highlighting how AI can help identify potential drug safety signals that warrant further investigation.
summary: Researchers analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and found users reporting increased appetite, sleep disturbances, and elevated heart rates after using unapproved versions of retatrutide. The symptom pattern differs from clinical trial results and shows how AI can help identify potential drug safety signals.
author: Science Daily

title: 15‑Minute Ultrasound Hydrodissection Offers Longer Relief for Carpal Tunnel Patients
content: A clinical trial of 63 patients found that ultrasound‑guided hydrodissection—a steroid‑free procedure that injects fluid to free a compressed wrist nerve—produced longer‑lasting reductions in pain, numbness and improved hand function compared with traditional steroid injections. Researchers suggest the treatment could help people with carpal tunnel syndrome avoid surgery.
summary: A 15‑minute, steroid‑free ultrasound‑guided hydrodissection procedure could offer lasting relief for carpal tunnel syndrome patients and help them avoid surgery. In a clinical trial of 63 patients, the procedure produced longer‑lasting improvements in pain, numbness, and hand function than traditional steroid injections.
author: Science Daily

title: Uncanny Valley episode covers Nathan Fielder and election office letters
content: This week’s episode of “Uncanny Valley” provides a behind-the-scenes look at the Nathan Fielder cover story. The discussion also addresses the generous promises made by tech billionaires and examines suspicious letters sent to US election offices.
summary: The latest episode of "Uncanny Valley" provides a behind-the-scenes look at the Nathan Fielder cover story. It also examines tech billionaires' generous promises and suspicious letters sent to US election offices.
author: Wired

title: Teenage Engineering EP-35 is a battery-powered instrument amp with built-in effects
content:
Teenage Engineering has introduced the EP-35, a battery-powered instrument amplifier designed for multiple inputs and instruments. The device features a line-in port, a 1/4-inch guitar input, and an XLR input for microphones, including those requiring phantom power. Users can also stream audio to the unit via Bluetooth.

The EP-35 supports connectivity between multiple units over Bluetooth using Auracast. When paired in stereo, tilting a unit to the left or right automatically assigns it to the corresponding stereo channel. The amplifier includes separate effects processors for both guitar and vocals, although the source notes that these effects are limited.
summary: The EP-35 is a multi-input, battery-powered amp featuring line-in, guitar, and XLR inputs with phantom power support. Users can stream audio via Bluetooth and pair multiple units using Auracast, with tilting a unit setting its stereo channel.
author: The Verge

title: SpaceX and Tesla form committees to discuss potential merger
content:
SpaceX and Tesla have established special committees to discuss a potential merger, a development that has drawn commentary regarding the companies’ financial and operational trajectories. The discourse surrounding the union often centers on the credibility of Elon Musk’s stated objectives, specifically his desire to go to Mars and "spread the light of consciousness," phrases he used during a recent SpaceX earnings call and in an earlier S-1 filing.

Critics of the proposed merger point to SpaceX’s high credit risk, noting that the company is preparing to borrow an additional $40 billion to purchase Nvidia chips. This financial strategy is contrasted with the technical feasibility of Musk’s space ambitions. The source argues that a reasonably informed perspective acknowledges that current technology, and even the raw information required to develop such technology, is insufficient to support human life in space.
summary: SpaceX and Tesla have established special committees to discuss a merger. SpaceX is also preparing to borrow $40 billion to purchase Nvidia chips.
author: The Verge

title: The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
content: On October 13th, Brendan Carr's FCC gave itself a new power - it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security. Today, it's exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain "foreign surveillance chips," the FCC claims. The agency doesn't say which specific gadgets it blocked, and it didn't immediately respond to our request for comment, but it does name the "surveillance chip": it's a HiVision Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC, a chip that turns a raw camera sensor into a home security camera, a dashcam, or the like. It's often s …
summary: On October 13th, Brendan Carr's FCC gave itself a new power - it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security. Today, it's exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain "foreign surveillance chips," the FCC claims.
author: The Verge

title: Meta revises terms but experts say AI can still scrape news sites
content:
Meta has modified its business terms to remove language that previously suggested it could freely train AI models on news sites, such as The Verge. However, legal experts argue these adjustments are insufficient to resolve their concerns. James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, told Nieman Lab that the changes do not restrict the "associated with your products or services" language, which would still permit Meta to scrape entire websites.

The new terms for business accounts, which take effect on October 30th, initially appeared to grant Meta permission to use news sites for AI training. Grimmelmann noted that the specific phrasing remains problematic, as it continues to allow for broad scraping activities despite the recent tweaks to the agreement.
summary: Meta has removed language from its business terms that suggested it could freely train AI models on news sites. Legal experts, including Cornell Law School professor James Grimmelmann, say the changes do not restrict language that could let Meta scrape entire sites and note the new terms take effect on October 30.
author: The Verge

title: PC shipments drop 21 percent YoY in Q3 2026 amid RAM price hikes
content:
Counterpoint Research reported that global PC shipments declined by 21 percent year-over-year in the third quarter of 2026, a figure consistent with earlier data from IDC and Omdia. The firm attributed this drop to rising component costs, noting that RAM, SSDs, and processors from Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have become more expensive over the past several months. These increases have driven price hikes across various devices, including MacBooks and Raspberry Pis.

The downturn marks a reversal for the PC market, which had experienced growth for over two years leading up to the second quarter of 2026. The component price surge also affected the broader consumer electronics sector, as smartphone shipments reached a 14-year low during the same quarter.
summary: Global PC shipments fell 21 percent year‑over‑year in the third quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. Counterpoint linked the decline to higher component prices, including rising costs for RAM, SSDs and chips.
author: The Verge

title: Canva launches Craft AI image model with two-stage planning architecture
content:
Canva has launched Canva Craft, a new AI image generation model designed to compete with offerings from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. According to a Thursday announcement, the model utilizes a two-stage architecture that plans a design before generating images, a process Canva says provides greater precision, consistency, and control.

The new tool can generate images at up to 2K resolution and supports more than 30 aspect ratios. While it is intended for creating social media posts and marketing content, Canva Craft is also capable of producing realistic scenes, digital art, and environmental imagery.
summary: Canva Craft uses a two-stage architecture to plan designs before generating images for greater precision and control. The model generates up to 2K resolution images in over 30 aspect ratios for various content types.
author: The Verge

title: Samsung all but confirms iPhone Duo is goosing Galaxy Z8 sales
content:
Samsung has indicated that its 2026 foldable lineup is experiencing significantly stronger sales compared to the previous year’s models. In a recent blog post, Samsung UK stated that combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are up 45 percent relative to the Galaxy Z Fold 7. The company did not provide specific sales figures for the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though it previously noted that larger foldables account for approximately 80 percent of total foldable purchases.

The timing of these sales increases aligns with recent industry developments. Samsung reported that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent during the week of September 6 to 12. This surge coincides with the September 9 announcement of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s entry into the folding phone market. Additionally, search volume for the Z Fold 8 increased by 260 percent throughout the entire month of September, which marks the launch period for the new devices. While Samsung did not explicitly mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its official release, the correlation between the announcement date and the spike in consumer interest is evident in the reported data.
summary: Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with the iPhone Duo.
author: Ars Technica

title: MAHA leader Calley Means resigns from Trump administration over food policy delays
content: Calley Means—a top ally to anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And a co-author of the so-called "MAHA bible"—resigned from his role in the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly in frustration over delays to food policy changes sought by the Make America Healthy Again movement. "I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy," Means wrote in a social media post this afternoon. "It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement." His post did not provide a reason for his departure. Means served as a senior advisor to Kennedy. Read full article Comments
summary: Calley Means—a top ally to anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
author: Ars Technica

title: German photographer wins 2026 Nikon Small World for inkjet droplet image
content:
Ole Bielfeldt, a 25-year-old German experimental photographer, has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. His winning image captures ink droplets being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer, a project that distinguished him from 1,802 other entries submitted from 69 countries. Bielfeldt discovered his interest in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown when he found an old microscope in his parents' attic. He subsequently taught himself the technique by building a custom adaptor from a tube and wood to connect the microscope to his father’s camera.

Capturing the rapid movement of ink droplets presented a significant technical challenge, as the drops moved faster than the camera’s standard shutter speed. To overcome this, Bielfeldt deconstructed the printer so that the paper moved beneath a stationary printhead. He then photographed the process in a dark room, using a flash to freeze the ink drops mid-air. Bielfeldt, who operates the photography and videography brand macrofying, relies on traditional techniques and does not use AI in his images.
summary: Ole Bielfeldt, a 25-year-old German experimental photographer, won the 2026 Nikon Small World competition with an image of ink droplets from an inkjet printer. He captured the fast-moving droplets by deconstructing the printer and using a flash to freeze the action in a dark room.
author: Ars Technica

title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
content:
Sharp declines in AI stocks, driven by rising datacenter and chip costs, pulled global markets lower on Thursday. The S&P 500 dropped 1.2%, marking its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite fell 2.6%. Despite this tech-led weakness, the broader US market showed resilience, with the majority of non-AI stocks rising. Consequently, the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 11 points, or less than 0.1%.

Simultaneously, oil prices reached their highest levels since May amid concerns regarding the war with Iran. The significant drop in the AI sector overwhelmed the positive performance of other market segments, resulting in a net negative outcome for major indices.
summary: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Midday news bulletin for October 22 2026 covers Europe and global stories
content: A midday news bulletin released on October 22, 2026 invites listeners to catch up on the most important stories from Europe and beyond. The bulletin covers the latest and breaking news across World, Business, Entertainment, Politics, Culture and Travel.
summary: The bulletin offers a roundup of the most important stories from Europe and beyond on October 22 2026. It includes coverage of world, business, entertainment, politics, culture and travel.
author: Euronews

title: Vance Urges Republicans to Stop Whining Over Ramaswamy Attack Ad in Ohio Governor Race
content:
US Vice President JD Vance defended an attack ad released by Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign in the Ohio governor’s race on Wednesday. Vance told fellow Republicans to "stop whining" about the advertisement and focus on winning the election. The ad features Donna Arthur, the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, who disputes Acton’s account of a childhood involving homelessness and sexual abuse. Arthur, whom Acton says she has not seen since 1978, urges Ohio voters not to support her daughter.

Acton has stated that she was sexually abused by her stepfather at age twelve. She noted that her mother remained with the stepfather, who was charged with rape but fled the state and was never tried before his death in 2004. Acton also claimed that she and her brother were removed from their mother's custody due to severe abuse, neglect, and sexual abuse, a narrative supported by her brother.
summary: Vance Urges Republicans to Stop Whining Over Ramaswamy Attack Ad in Ohio Governor Race.
author: France 24

title: Israel’s Ben‑Gvir uses AI videos to mock Gazans as “donkeys” and send them to Paris
content:
Israel’s far‑right minister Itamar Ben‑Gvir has released a series of AI‑generated videos that mock Palestinians and push political messages ahead of the country’s election. The clips include scenes that magically transport Gazans to Paris and label them “donkeys” for choosing to stay in Gaza.

One of the videos has triggered an online spat with France. The incident highlights the growing use of AI in the campaign, as parties employ deepfakes, bots and other AI‑generated content, raising concerns about disinformation and the technology’s influence on voters.
summary: Israel’s far‑right minister Itamar Ben‑Gvir is using AI‑generated videos to mock Palestinians, including transporting Gazans to Paris and calling them “donkeys” for staying. The videos have sparked an online spat with France and raise concerns about AI‑driven disinformation in the election campaign.
author: France 24

title: Paris Imposes Nightly Curfew in Select Areas Until Monday
content:
A curfew has been extended in selected areas of Paris, effective every night from 11:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. The restriction remains in place until Monday morning. The measure, issued by the Paris police prefecture and published on Thursday, was put in force following the violence and looting that occurred over the weekend.

The same day, a student‑organized protest in Paris proceeded with hundreds in attendance. The demonstration had followed four weeks of earlier protests before the October 17 rallies. A police ban on the event was lifted after an emergency court injunction, allowing the protest to take place. FRANCE 24’s Mark Owen spoke with Alice Cohen‑Morzadec, International Spokesperson of “L’Union étudiante.”
summary: The curfew has been extended in certain areas of Paris, every night from 11:00 p. M.
author: France 24

title: Can weak economic growth threaten Europe's sophisticated social system?
content:
Europe faces the challenge of maintaining one of the world’s most ambitious social systems while its economic growth lags behind major competitors.  

The issue, according to former European Commissioner for Trade and former World Trade Organization Director‑General Pascal Lamy, lies at the core of the continent’s rising economic and political tensions.  

Lamy argues that the problem extends beyond France’s current turmoil, pointing to a widening gap between Europe’s social commitments and its ability to generate the economic growth required to sustain them.
summary: Pascal Lamy, former European Commissioner for Trade and former WTO Director-General, says Europe faces a widening disconnect between its social commitments and its ability to generate the economic growth needed to sustain them. He argues that this gap threatens the continent's ability to maintain its ambitious social model amid mounting economic and political tensions.
author: France 24

title: Tom Skerritt, Emmy‑winning actor known for 'Top Gun' and 'Picket Fences', dies at 93
content: US actor Tom Skerritt, known for his roles as the doomed caption in 1979's "Alien", a tough flight instructor in the 1986 megahit “Top Gun” and who won an Emmy award winner for his work in the television series “Picket Fences”, has died at 93, his family said in a statement.
summary: US actor Tom Skerritt, known for his roles in "Alien", "Top Gun", and the Emmy‑winning series "Picket Fences", died at 93. His family said he died in a statement.
author: France 24

title: 7.0 Earthquake Hits Remote Tibet Region, 16 Dead
content:
A 7.0‑magnitude earthquake struck China’s remote Tibet region on Thursday, according to state media. The tremor was strong enough to trigger widespread damage across the area.

At least 16 people have died and dozens more were injured, with hundreds of houses collapsing in the quake’s aftermath.
summary: At least 16 people died and dozens more were injured after a 7.0 earthquake struck China’s remote Tibet region on Thursday, according to state media. Hundreds of houses collapsed during the tremor.
author: France 24

title: UAE Nominates Former Envoy Lana Nusseibeh as UN Secretary General Amid Human Rights Concerns
content: The United Arab Emirates has nominated former envoy Lana Nusseibeh for UN Secretary‑General. Human‑rights defenders warn that appointing a diplomat from a country with a questionable human‑rights record and accusations of supporting forces behind a Sudan massacre could spell catastrophe for the UN.
summary: UAE Nominates Former Envoy Lana Nusseibeh as UN Secretary General Amid Human Rights Concerns.
author: France 24

title: EU deepens ties with Vietnam amid human rights and labor concerns
content:
The European Union and Vietnam are expanding their economic and diplomatic relationship.  

This closer cooperation has sparked concerns that Brussels may not be sufficiently addressing Hanoi’s human rights record, labor standards, and trade imbalances.
summary: The EU and Vietnam are deepening economic and diplomatic ties. Closer cooperation raises concerns about whether Brussels is doing enough to address Hanoi's human rights record, labor standards, and trade imbalances.
author: DW World

title: Albanian prime minister blames "antifa" for growing student anti-corruption protests
content: As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.
summary: Albanian prime minister blames "antifa" for growing student anti-corruption protests.
author: DW World

title: Ebola responders in DRC under pressure as outbreak reaches eighth province
content: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to an eighth province, prompting heightened pressure on responders as the disease expands. On Thursday, investigators pursued all leads to evaluate the risk of further transmission into Nigeria.
summary: Ebola responders in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) are under pressure as the deadly outbreak reaches an eighth province. Investigators pursued all leads on Thursday to assess the risk of the disease spreading to Nigeria.
author: UN News

title: Raye wins 2026 Mercury Prize for album This Music May Contain Hope
content: Singer who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band album Raye is the winner of the 2026 Mercury prize, for her second studio album, This Music May Contain Hope. Her win – for a hugely ambitious 73-minute record that spanned big band jazz, power balladry, funk and more – caps an ongoing renaissance for a British singer who at one point was in the doldrums, lashing out publicly at her record label for not letting her release a studio album.
summary: Raye was named the winner of the 2026 Mercury Prize for her second studio album, This Music May Contain Hope. The 73‑minute record blends big‑band jazz, power balladry and funk, adding to her record‑breaking Brit Awards success.
author: Guardian World

title: Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer
content:
Burnham is set to reveal government plans for an AI‑driven “Cobra” unit that will detect wildfires, a move prompted by this year’s record‑breaking heat and the resulting blazes across the United Kingdom. The prime minister will also announce funding for specialised protective gear and the deployment of military aircraft to support firefighting efforts.

The summer was the hottest on record, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fueling fires that triggered an emergency mobile‑phone alert in England and Wales. Figures released on 8 October show a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.
summary: Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer.
author: Guardian World

title: Aisha Zaman charged after police officer shot in Nottingham city centre
content: A 27‑year‑old woman, Aisha Zaman of Nottingham’s Hyson Green area, has been charged after a police officer was shot while responding to an incident in the city centre on Sunday. Zaman faces two firearms charges: possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence. The charges stem directly from the shooting of the officer during the Sunday incident.
summary: A 27-year-old woman was charged after a police officer was shot while attending an incident in Nottingham city centre on Sunday. Aisha Zaman of Hyson Green was charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.
author: Guardian World

title: Kim Aris talks to detained Aung San Suu Kyi for first time in over five years
content:
The son of Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi has spoken to his mother for the first time in more than five years, following a loosening of detention restrictions.

Kim Aris posted on Facebook that he was finally able to speak with his mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. He said that hearing her voice again means more than words can express.
summary: Kim Aris said he was finally able to speak with his mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. He posted on Facebook that hearing her voice again means more than words can express.
author: Guardian World

title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Gulf attacks threaten supply
content:
Oil prices rose to a five‑month high on Thursday after attacks in Saudi Arabia and incidents involving tankers in the Strait of Hormuz raised concerns about further disruptions to global crude supplies. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it struck four vessels in the northern Gulf and that three additional vessels hit mines near the strait.

The benchmark Brent crude increased 3%, reaching $112 a barrel, the first time it had traded at that level since 18 May. The price jump reflects market reactions to the reported maritime attacks and the perceived threat to oil flow from the region.
summary: Iran’s IRGC said it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the Strait of Hormuz, prompting oil prices to rise to a five‑month high. Brent crude rose 3% to $112 a barrel, its highest level since 18 May.
author: Guardian World

title: Billionaire Reform donor Sasan Ghandehari linked to Iranian religious foundation
content:
An exclusive report says billionaire donor Sasan Ghandehari, also known as Hossein Ghandehari, previously partnered with a powerful Iranian religious foundation that operates under the authority of Iran’s supreme leader. The piece notes that this connection has prompted questions about his past dealings with the hard‑line republic.

Ghandehari, described as little known in the UK until recently, pledged to give millions to Reform UK and donated £50,000 to Nigel Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.
summary: Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor, Hossein “Sasan” Ghandehari, was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader. Ghandehari, previously little known in the UK, pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage for two Davos World Economic Forum passes.
author: Guardian World

title: First human case of Shamonda virus identified in France
content:
A man in France has become the first known human case of Shamonda virus, a bunyavirus transmitted by bites from infected midges. Authorities are investigating whether the virus, which is typically found in livestock, contributed to the man’s death.

The Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety notes that in cattle, sheep and goats the virus can cause diarrhoea, loss of appetite, reduced milk production, abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn animals. Investigations continue to determine the role of the virus in the fatal human infection.
summary: A man in France has become the first known human to contract Shamonda virus, a bunyavirus spread by bites from infected midges. Investigations are under way to determine whether the virus, which can cause diarrhoea, loss of appetite, reduced milk yield, abortions and congenital abnormalities in cattle, sheep and goats, contributed to his death.
author: Guardian World

title: Lewis Hamilton wants to race until early 2030s to compete in Rwanda's African Grand Prix
content:
Lewis Hamilton, the 41‑year‑old seven‑time Formula One world champion, has said he hopes to keep racing until the early 2030s so he can compete in the African Grand Prix. Hamilton described the event as a “dream” and said he believes it is right for F1 to hold a race in Rwanda despite criticism of the country’s human‑rights record.

Formula One confirmed that Rwanda will host the African Grand Prix after a ten‑year agreement was reached for a purpose‑built circuit. The venue will be in Bugesera, about 25 miles south of Kigali, and the first race is scheduled for the early 2030s. The event will mark the sport’s return to Africa for the first time since the 1993 Grand Prix at Kyalami in South Africa.
summary: Lewis Hamilton wants to race until early 2030s to compete in Rwanda's African Grand Prix.
author: Guardian World

title: Seth Meyers mocks JD Vance as having charisma of wet ham
content: Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s seeming cognitive decline and Vance’s rock-bottom approval ratings Late-night hosts recapped a tough couple of days for the Oval Office, as Donald Trump waved to an imaginary crowd and JD Vance bombed softball interviews.
summary: Seth Meyers described JD Vance as having the integrity of a used-car salesman and the charisma of a wet ham. Late-night hosts also discussed Donald Trump's seeming cognitive decline and Vance's low approval ratings.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Glee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America? | Alim Kheraj
content: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs For months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee. In July, he expressed his love for the musical comedy drama he created. In September, he said that he had finished writing a pilot for a potential reboot, adding that he had reached out to some of the cast about a reunion. And now it is official : Disney+ and Hulu have commissioned a Glee revival. Glee, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015, was a cultural juggernaut during its initial tenure. The show won six Emmys, four Golden Globes and made stars of actors including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss and the late Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera. Centred on the trials of New Directions, a scrappy show choir at the fictional McKinley high school in Ohio, the show became known for its peppy covers of show tunes, 80s power pop hits such as Journey’s Don’t Stop Believin’ (a Glee signature), 2010s chart-toppers and some truly baffling mashups (the amalgamation of Scissor Sisters’ Let’s Have a Kiki and Turkey Lurkey Time from Promises, Promises remains … a choice).
summary: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs For months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’
content: Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker • This article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I? • Review: Ali G: Who Iz I? The chair of the El Paso County Republican Party has said he intends to sue Sacha Baron Cohen over footage of the local politician used in new satirical comedy Ali G: Who Iz I? In the film, Michael Aboud is shown taking part in a training programme with another Cohen character, ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, who instructs Aboud and fellow Maga sympathisers in self-defence techniques including the wearing, over clothes, of protective plastic buttocks. title: Sri Lanka chase 430 to beat England despite Brook's record ODI 202
content:

The result came despite England captain Harry Brook scoring the fastest double century in ODI history, as his record innings proved insufficient to secure a win for his team.

The match featured a dramatic turnaround for Sri Lanka, who recovered from an early collapse of 24 for two. Pavan Rathnayake top-scored with 130 runs, while Dasun Shanaka and Avishka Fernando both contributed 97. Shanaka’s aggressive performance included eight sixes, helping the team overcome its initial struggles. Although England briefly regained momentum late in the innings, Sri Lanka secured the victory with one ball to spare. The final over saw Liyanage hit a six to complete the chase, cementing the historic nature of the contest.
summary: Sri Lanka successfully chased a target of 430 in Rawalpindi, achieving the second-highest chase in ODI history to defeat England. England captain Harry Brook scored the fastest double century in ODI history, but Sri Lanka's innings, led by Pavan Rathnayake's 130, secured the win.

title: Three things you should know about permafrost
content:
Three things you should know about permafrost

Permafrost, the permanently frozen layer of soil that lies beneath roughly 15 % of land in the Northern Hemisphere, has been largely overlooked in climate discussions. It was formed mainly during the last ice age, trapping organic material that has remained locked away for thousands of years. As global temperatures rise, this material is thawing, allowing microbes to break down the organic matter and release carbon dioxide and methane—both powerful greenhouse gases that accelerate warming. The Arctic permafrost area has already shrunk by about 12 % since 1850, and the rate of loss has accelerated over the past 50 years. Yet most models used in United Nations climate reports include only the gradual loss of permafrost, omitting the abrupt thaw and collapse that can follow heat waves and fires. Because of this omission, scientists warn that current projections may underestimate how quickly the planet could warm.

Wildfires, a natural component of boreal forest ecosystems, are becoming more intense due to climate change. These fires can speed up permafrost thaw, potentially releasing the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by the end of the century. In remote parts of Canada and Alaska, the prevailing policy is to allow fires to burn unless they threaten human habitats. Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are mapping burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, identifying areas where fires are likely to spread and where specific permafrost types—such as the deep, carbon‑dense Yedoma from the late Pleistocene—could release the most emissions. Proposed responses include prescribed fires, a practice used by Indigenous groups for millennia to reduce the risk of large blazes, as well as early detection and suppression efforts.

The carbon cycle of permafrost is highly complex. Approximately 1.5 trillion tons of carbon are stored in permafrost, roughly twice the amount in the atmosphere. While thawing releases greenhouse gases, other processes may offset some of that loss. For instance, as temperatures rise, plants can expand northward, sequestering atmospheric carbon as they grow. Researchers are still working to quantify how much carbon is lost from thaw and how much can be recovered, taking into account factors such as fire severity, local climate, and permafrost type. The more the planet warms, the more these intertwined natural phenomena will challenge our understanding. This article appears in The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter.
summary: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.

title: Making the case for context-aware AI
content: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes. For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know. The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling. This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents. Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis. Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized. Two words for you: context matters. My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis. Welcome, Devavrat. Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here. Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises. The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision. Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come. Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there. Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one. In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom. Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization? Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better. Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision. Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer? Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate. Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that. Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it. And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it. Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two? Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that. On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go. And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time. The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner. Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well? Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one. Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this. And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed. Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about? Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one. Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak. And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly. Megan: That’d be fantastic, wouldn’t it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you’ll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. summary: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one.

title: Microsoft says its AI tool diagnoses conditions up to four times more accurately than doctors
content:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman announced that the company has developed an AI-powered tool capable of diagnosing medical conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors. Suleyman described this development as the realization of a long-held promise by AI leaders to improve lives through healthcare applications. The company’s findings were published in the journal Science on Thursday.

The study’s results are based on tests comparing Microsoft’s AI system against human physicians using scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. To conduct these comparisons, Microsoft compiled the cases into its own benchmark.
summary: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman said the company has created an AI-powered diagnostic tool that can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors. title: Tesla in Full Self-Driving mode kills 71-year-old crossing I-80 in Vallejo
content:
A 71‑year‑old man was killed after being hit by a Tesla operating in Full Self‑Driving (FSD) mode while crossing Interstate 80 in Vallejo, California, at approximately 2:30 a.m. on Thursday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. The California Highway Patrol said a dash‑cam video showed the Tesla applying its brakes and steering left in an attempt to avoid the pedestrian, yet the vehicle’s right‑front portion struck the man.

The CHP added that authorities believe at least one additional vehicle may have struck the pedestrian after the Tesla, though further details were not provided.
summary: A 71-year-old man was fatally struck by a Tesla operating in Full Self-Driving mode while crossing I-80 in Vallejo, California at about 2:30 AM on Thursday. Dash‑cam video showed the vehicle braking and steering left before its right front portion hit the pedestrian, and authorities believe another vehicle also struck the man after the Tesla.

title: EA shuts down BioWare, cancels Mass Effect game; leaked trailer appears on Reddit

A trailer that appears to represent the cancelled title was posted on Reddit today. The video is labeled “in‑engine footage” and uses “pre‑production assets,” according to a message at its start. It centers on an ex‑soldier speaking with a mysterious Asari character who approaches him at a bar, and it includes a flashback to a fight that echoes the gameplay of the original Mass Effect trilogy. title: Delta 2.0 emulator update adds iPhone Duo optimization and new features
content:
The Delta gaming emulator has been updated to version 2.0, bringing a range of new features and support enhancements. Among the additions are Sega Genesis game compatibility, animated controller skins, custom Pokémon DLC experiences, and a redesigned user interface built around “Liquid Glass.”  

A key focus of the update is optimization for Apple’s iPhone Duo, a foldable device with a shape reminiscent of a Nintendo DS. summary: Delta 2.0 adds support for Apple’s iPhone Duo and includes Sega Genesis games, animated controller skins, custom Pokémon DLC experiences, and a UI built for Liquid Glass. title: UNEP says 1.5°C limit already exceeded, shifts focus to limiting overshoot
content:
In 2015, all but two countries agreed to try to keep global temperatures from rising more than 1.5 °C above pre‑industrial levels. Since that agreement, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) says most nations have treated the target as aspirational, and the United States has alternately withdrawn from and recommitted to the pact.  

On Wednesday, UNEP announced that it no longer considers keeping warming below 1.5 °C a viable goal. The agency now proposes to focus on limiting both the duration and magnitude of any overshoot of the 1.5 °C threshold. Achieving that, UNEP says, will require dramatic emissions cuts immediately and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the end of the century.  

The organization notes that, depending on the baseline and temperature reconstruction used, the world is either very close to or has already exceeded the 1.5 °C milestone, and that the exceptionally strong current El Niño event is likely to push temperatures over the limit regardless of the record chosen.
summary: UNEP acknowledged that keeping global warming below 1.5°C is no longer viable. It said future action must limit the duration and magnitude of any overshoot, requiring dramatic emissions cuts and removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of CO₂ before the end of the century.
author: Ars Technica

title: 300+ Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH and capture plaintext email
content:
A researcher reported on Tuesday that unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and altered them to favor unencrypted email traffic while redirecting SSH connections through servers under the attackers’ control. The intrusion began in late August, according to Tor volunteers, when the perpetrators used a reused valid password to gain access to a Tor management server.

After breaching the management server, the attackers installed Ebury, a Linux backdoor first identified 12 years ago. They then connected from that server to a second Tor server named Switzerland2 via SSH, employing an RSA key that investigators could not locate among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative access to Switzerland2, the attackers also deployed Ebury on that system.

Finally, the intruders reconfigured the settings of two exit nodes hosted on Switzerland2, completing the manipulation of the compromised Tor infrastructure.
summary: 300+ Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH and capture plaintext email.
author: Ars Technica

title: GM says it remains all‑in on EVs and autonomy as Super Cruise expands to most models
content:
General Motors used its recent GM Forward event to reaffirm its commitment to electrification, autonomous driving and vehicle quality. Executives said the company’s “hands‑off, eyes‑off” Super Cruise system will be broadened to almost the entire model range, extending beyond the Escalade IQ announced last year to include pickup trucks and crossovers.

Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, noted that Super Cruise is being tested at a rate of one million miles (approximately 1.6 million km) each month in both virtual simulations and real‑world driving. The company framed this effort as part of a broader goal for vehicles to not only transport occupants but also perform additional tasks for them.

Ars Technica disclosed that GM covered its travel from Detroit to New York and lodging to attend the event, and clarified that the outlet does not accept paid editorial content. The announcement underscores GM’s intention to stay “all‑in” on electric vehicles and autonomous technology despite external criticism.
summary: At the GM Forward event, executives announced that the hands‑off Super Cruise system will be rolled out to nearly every vehicle, including trucks and crossovers, with testing at about 1 million miles per month. title: VBoy Color emulator adds full-color palette to Nintendo Virtual Boy games
content:
A new emulator called VBoy Color expands on the earlier Red Viper Virtual Boy emulator by introducing a tile‑based palette system that supports many more colors in each frame. According to the emulator’s readme files, game‑specific “Color Packs” can assign a distinct four‑color palette to each 8×8 tile, rather than merely swapping the original four shades of red for four different hues.

The approach lets the emulator differentiate objects that shared the same red tones in the original hardware. For example, in Mario Clash the emulator can render green pipes, grey platforms and red brick walls with separate palettes, and in titles such as Jack Bros. or Vertical Force it improves contrast between the player character and busy red backgrounds. The resulting visuals are described as reminiscent of a Game Boy Color‑style display, as if Nintendo had originally equipped the Virtual Boy with a full‑color screen.
summary: VBoy Color is an emulator that uses a tile‑based palette system to assign a distinct four‑color palette to each 8×8 tile in Virtual Boy games. This lets titles such as Mario Clash, Jack Bros. and Vertical Force display many more colors and improve contrast compared with the original red‑on‑red display.

title: Guinea-Bissau rejects US‑funded hepatitis B newborn vaccine trial
content:
Government officials in Guinea‑Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be conducted by Danish researchers and financed by the United States. The study was intended to investigate alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, a dose that is currently recommended worldwide and has been used safely for decades.

In an email to Ars Technica, lead researcher Christine Stabell Benn of the Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark said that Guinea‑Bissau’s Council of Ministers “formally reaffirmed its non‑acceptance of the study on 16 October.” The rejection was reported after judicial police in the country raided the Bandim Health offices and seized vaccines; the police action followed the council’s decision.
summary: Government officials in Guinea‑Bissau formally rejected a US‑funded clinical trial by Danish researchers that aimed to investigate alleged nonspecific harms of the newborn hepatitis B vaccine. The Council of Ministers reaffirmed its non‑acceptance on 16 October, and judicial police subsequently raided the Bandim Health Project offices and seized vaccines.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion fine after New Mexico rejects settlement
content:
A jury in New Mexico found Meta guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer‑protection laws, ordering the company to pay a $25 billion fine. The penalty is the largest ever imposed on Meta, according to the court’s ruling.

The fine followed New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s decision not to join an $18 billion settlement that Meta had reached earlier this year with attorneys general in almost every other state. Torrez’s refusal left New Mexico to pursue its own case against the tech giant.

In his opinion issued Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew noted that there is no “bright line rule” for setting a penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 over issues such as data control, third‑party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.
summary: Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found it guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws. The penalty follows New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s decision not to join an $18 billion multistate settlement Meta reached earlier this year.

content: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft’s system itself.
summary: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. Most of the improvement appears to come from the AI models underneath rather than Microsoft’s system itself.

title: Finland orders Google to halt work after illegal felling of 250,000 trees
content: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone. After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.
summary: Google was ordered to stop work at two sites in Finland after it illegally cleared about 250,000 trees from a 330‑hectare forest near Muhos to build a datacentre. Residents say brown water from the cleared site is flowing into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Big tech backlash over datacenters and AI fuels US midterm sentiment
content: Datacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it has soured Americans on big tech How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions The campaign ad begins with a clear, idyllic stream that suddenly turns sludge-brown as two concrete datacenters slam onto its banks. Another facility thuds down on a peaceful suburban park, and two more crush-green pastures as an ominous soundtrack to a disaster movie blares overtop. “They’re coming for our rivers. Our neighborhoods. Our farmland,” a deep-voiced narrator says. “Because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee.”
summary: Americans have soured on big tech because of datacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it. A campaign ad blames a law written by Brent Taylor for allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee, showing environmental damage.

title: The Audacity TV series satirizes AI tech titans with Succession‑style drama
content: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat. This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.”
summary: The Audacity TV series satirizes AI tech titans with Succession‑style drama.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Meta agrees to keep Mark Zuckerberg in California for eight years to aid tax bill
content: Meta announced that it has reached an agreement with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to assist him with a possible California wealth tax aimed at billionaires. Under the deal, Zuckerberg has agreed to remain in California for eight years, even if the state enacts a one‑off 5 % wealth tax. The arrangement was disclosed Wednesday night by the social‑media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, and it ties the executive’s residency to Meta’s headquarters location in the state.
summary: Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him cover a possible one‑off 5% California wealth tax aimed at billionaires. The arrangement requires Zuckerberg to remain in California for eight years, keeping the company’s chief executive in the state where Meta’s headquarters are located.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Websites worldwide face millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
content:
Websites around the globe have experienced millions of attempts to exploit a newly disclosed vulnerability in the PHP programming language, according to cybersecurity firms. The flaw, which affects the language that underpins roughly 70 % of all websites, was first reported on Wednesday.

In response, several governments and private companies have taken their sites offline to apply patches before any successful attacks could occur. U.S. officials have warned that the vulnerability could enable attackers to seize control of web servers, exfiltrate data and disrupt services. The coordinated pull‑offline actions aim to mitigate those risks while the PHP code is being corrected.
summary: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault Tell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw? What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?
author: Guardian Technology

title: Nine killed in Russian missile and drone attacks across Ukraine in 24 hours
content: At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past 24 hours, Ukrainian authorities said. Overnight missile and drone strikes caused fires in Kyiv and in the Kharkiv region.
summary: At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past 24 hours, according to Ukrainian authorities. Overnight missile and drone strikes sparked fires in Kyiv and the Kharkiv region.

title: Gulf nations fear renewed US‑Iran war amid election volatility
content: Gulf nations are preparing for a possible return to all‑out war between the United States and Iran. Heightened volatility surrounding the Israeli and U.S. midterm elections is prompting fears that the United States and Israel could launch a short, intensive strike campaign against Iran to force concessions, while Iran has vowed a devastating response against the Gulf states.
summary: Gulf nations fear renewed US‑Iran war amid election volatility.

title: Art Basel Paris proceeds with galleries and artists as security tightened after protests
content: Art Basel Paris has drawn international galleries and contemporary artists to the Grand Palais. In response to violent protests in the capital, organisers have increased security measures around the prestigious art fair.

content: Families of more than 4,000 Azerbaijanis who remain missing since the first Karabakh war have appealed to European Union institutions for answers. They hope that the ongoing peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan will finally clarify the fate of their relatives.

title: French interfac student movement stages protests during school holidays
content: French students organized new protests on Thursday, led by the interfac student movement, even though it is currently the school holidays in France. Student representatives are set to meet soon with Education Minister Edouard Geffray. The story was reported by FRANCE 24's Ellen Gainsford.

title: Ethiopia takes Zalambessa as tensions rise over possible war with Eritrea
content: Concerns are mounting as Ethiopia and Eritrea appear to be inching closer to war. Ethiopia has recently taken control of the border town of Zalambessa, heightening fears that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed may deploy troops into Eritrea. In a recent interview for In Perspective, Martin Plaut, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Commonwealth Studies at the University of London, discussed the situation.
summary: Ethiopia has taken control of the border town of Zalambessa, heightening concerns of a wider conflict with Eritrea. Analysts, including senior research fellow Martin Plaut of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies, warn that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed could order troops into Eritrea.

title: Georgia Democrats rally Black vote against Trump's redistricting and election law
content: President Donald Trump’s efforts to redraw congressional maps and a Georgia state election law that disproportionately affect African Americans are intended to dilute the Black vote. Six decades after Atlanta’s pivotal role in the civil‑rights movement that secured voting rights for Blacks in the South, the community is actively resisting these changes.
summary: President Donald Trump's push to redistrict congressional maps and a Georgia state election law that disproportionately affect African Americans are aimed at diluting the Black vote. Six decades after Atlanta's civil‑rights era, the Black community in Georgia is fighting back.

title: Ukraine and Russia exchange drone and missile strikes, seven killed in Ukraine
content: Ukraine and Russia carried out drone and missile strikes on Thursday, killing seven people in Ukraine, authorities said. Moscow reported intercepting 630 Ukrainian drones aimed at the Russian capital. The attacks occurred hours after U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, during which Witkoff said Moscow was ready to resume trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington.
summary: Ukraine and Russia exchanged drone and missile strikes on Thursday, killing seven people in Ukraine, according to authorities. Moscow said it had intercepted 630 Ukrainian drones targeting the Russian capital.
